content: The analysis determined that the certainty of evidence for sensitivity was very low. There were significant concerns regarding the indirectness of specificity, primarily due to the limited number of rifampicin-resistant cases, most of which originated from India and Peru. The diagnostic accuracy of the Molbio Truenat tuberculosis and rifampicin-resistance assays was evaluated in their intended settings. For pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) in adults, the Molbio Truenat MTB test was compared to the microbiological reference standard (MRS). The results showed high true negative (TN) rates with minimal false positives (FP). However, a meta-analysis for specificity could not be conducted due to data variability. The Molbio Truenat MTB Plus test was also assessed for its diagnostic accuracy in detecting pulmonary TB in adults compared to MRS. Similar to the MTB test, it demonstrated high TN rates with low FP rates. For rifampicin resistance detection, the Molbio Truenat MTB-RIF Dx test was evaluated in adults. The test showed moderate diagnostic accuracy, with high TN rates and low FP rates. A cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted to compare the costs, affordability, and cost-effectiveness of implementing the Truenat MTB, MTB Plus, and MTB-RIF Dx systems. A systematic review of economic evaluations of molecular-based tests for active TB diagnosis, including the Truenat MTB test, was performed. Only one study specifically assessed the cost-effectiveness of the Truenat MTB test, suggesting it is likely cost-effective if implemented at the point of care in India. However, this study relied on several modeling assumptions, such as improved linkage to care and increased treatment initiation, which should be validated in pragmatic trials. Generalizing cost-effectiveness findings across different settings requires caution, as local implementation conditions and settings must be considered. From a user perspective, qualitative research results based on Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra tests indicated that diagnostic accuracy and usability might vary across patient populations. Additionally, supply chain and maintenance requirements for program staff and managers may differ. The Truenat implementation trial revealed that laboratory technicians generally found the test acceptable and feasible, though some noted it was more complex to perform compared to Xpert MTB/RIF. Operational research is needed to ensure optimal use of these tests in their intended settings. Further evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of Truenat (MTB, MTB Plus, and MTB-RIF) in specific patient populations, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV), former TB patients, and those with extrapulmonary TB, is recommended. Moderate complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for TB and rifampicin/isoniazid resistance detection are increasingly available. These tests are faster and less complex than phenotypic culture-based drug susceptibility testing (DST) and line-probe assays (LPA). They are largely automated after the sample preparation step and may serve as initial tests for detecting TB and resistance to first-line TB drugs (rifampicin and isoniazid). These technologies are particularly suited for high-population-density areas with rapid sample referral systems. The WHO Global TB Programme initiated an update of guidelines and commissioned a systematic review on the use of moderate complexity automated NAATs for TB and drug resistance detection. Three PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) questions were designed to guide the evidence search and analysis. These questions addressed the use of moderate complexity automated NAATs for detecting pulmonary TB, rifampicin resistance, and isoniazid resistance in respiratory samples compared to culture-based phenotypic DST. A comprehensive search of databases (PubMed, Embase, BIOSIS, Web of Science, LILACS, and Cochrane) was conducted for studies published between January 2009 and July 2020. Diagnostic companies were contacted for internal validation data, and studies from the WHO public call for data submission were included. Mycobacterial culture was used as the reference standard for TB detection, while resistance detection was compared to phenotypic DST and a composite reference standard combining phenotypic and genotypic DST results. Meta-analyses were performed to obtain pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates for rifampicin resistance, isoniazid resistance, and TB detection. Descriptive analyses were conducted when only a limited number of studies were available.
